p.src: Now when Cao Ren saw Lord Guan fall from his horse, he led his troops charging out of the city; but Guan Ping drove them back with a fierce assault, rescued Lord Guan to the camp, and drew the arrow from his arm. The arrowhead had been poisoned; the toxin had entered the bone, and his right arm was blue, swollen, and immobile. In alarm, Guan Ping conferred with the other generals: “If Father loses the use of this arm, how can he face the enemy? We had better return temporarily to Jingzhou so that he may recover.” Thereupon they entered Lord Guan’s tent together. He asked, “What brings you here?” They replied, “Seeing Your Lordship’s injured right arm, we fear that anger in battle may cause further harm and hinder you in the charge. We have agreed that the army should temporarily withdraw to Jingzhou while you recover.” Lord Guan angrily said, “Fan Castle is almost within my grasp; once I take it, I shall press swiftly onward straight to Xudu, destroy the traitor Cao, and bring peace to the House of Han. How could I let a minor wound ruin a great undertaking? Would you dare weaken my army’s resolve?” Guan Ping and the others withdrew in silence.

p.src: Seeing that Lord Guan would neither withdraw nor recover from his wound, the generals had no choice but to seek renowned physicians everywhere. One day, a man suddenly arrived from Jiangdong in a small boat and came directly before the camp. A junior officer brought him before Guan Ping. Guan Ping observed that the man wore a square cap and loose robe and carried a green medicine bag on his arm; he introduced himself as a native of Qiao County in the state of Pei, surnamed Hua, named Tuo, and styled Yuanhua. “I heard that General Guan, a hero of the realm, has been struck by a poisoned arrow, so I have come expressly to treat him.” Guan Ping asked, “Are you not the physician who once treated Zhou Tai of Eastern Wu?” Hua Tuo replied, “I am.” Overjoyed, Guan Ping and the generals immediately escorted Hua Tuo into the tent to see Lord Guan. Lord Guan’s arm was aching at the time, but fearing any weakening of his army’s morale and having no other diversion, he was playing weiqi with Ma Liang; hearing that a physician had arrived, he summoned him in at once. After courtesies were exchanged, Hua Tuo was given a seat. When tea was finished, Hua Tuo asked to examine the arm. Lord Guan bared his robe and extended his arm for Hua Tuo’s inspection. Hua Tuo said, “This wound was made by a crossbow bolt coated with aconite poison, which has penetrated to the bone; unless treated soon, this arm will become useless.” Lord Guan asked, “What will you use to treat it?” Hua Tuo replied, “I have a method of my own. I fear only that Your Lordship may be afraid.” Lord Guan laughed. “I regard death as a return home. What have I to fear?” Hua Tuo said, “In a quiet place, a post must be erected with a large ring nailed to it. Your Lordship must pass your arm through the ring and have it bound with rope, after which your head must be covered with a quilt. I shall cut through the flesh with a sharp knife down to the bone, scrape away the arrow poison from it, apply medicine, and stitch the wound with thread; only then will all be well. I fear only that Your Lordship may be afraid.” Lord Guan laughed. “If it is so simple, what need is there for post and ring?” He ordered a banquet prepared for Hua Tuo.

p.src: After drinking several cups of wine, Lord Guan continued his game with Ma Liang while extending his arm for Hua Tuo to cut. Hua Tuo took a sharp knife in hand and ordered a junior officer to hold a large basin beneath the arm to catch the blood. Hua Tuo said, “I shall begin now. Your Lordship, do not be alarmed.” Lord Guan replied, “Treat me as you see fit. Am I to be compared with common men who fear pain?” Hua Tuo then cut through flesh to the bone, which had already turned blue; when he scraped the bone with his knife, it made a rasping sound. All who watched inside and outside the tent covered their faces and turned pale. Yet Lord Guan drank wine, ate meat, talked, laughed, and played weiqi without the least sign of pain. Before long, blood filled the basin. Hua Tuo scraped away all the poison, applied medicine, and stitched the wound with thread. Lord Guan rose with a great laugh and told the generals, “This arm moves and stretches as before, and there is no pain at all. Sir, you truly are a divine physician!” Hua Tuo said, “In all my life as a physician, I have never seen such a thing. Your Lordship is truly a god from heaven!” A later poet wrote:

p.src: When Lord Guan’s arrow wound had healed, he prepared a banquet to thank Hua Tuo warmly. Hua Tuo said, “Though Your Lordship’s wound has been treated, you must take care of it. Above all, do not let anger disturb the injury. After a hundred days, it will be completely restored.” Lord Guan offered him a hundred taels of gold as reward. Hua Tuo said, “I heard of Your Lordship’s lofty righteousness and came expressly to treat you. How could I have hoped for payment?” He firmly declined the reward, left a packet of medicine to apply to the wound, then took his leave and departed.

p.src: Now Lord Guan’s capture of Yu Jin and execution of Pang De greatly magnified his fame, and all the realm stood in awe. Scouts carried the news to Xudu. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed and assembled his civil and military officers for counsel. “I have always known that Yunchang’s wisdom and valor are unequaled. Now that he holds Jingzhou and Xiangyang, he is like a tiger given wings. Yu Jin has been captured, Pang De slain, and the mettle of Wei’s army blunted; what are we to do if he leads his army straight to Xudu? I intend to move the capital to avoid him.” Sima Yi remonstrated, “You must not. Yu Jin and the others were overwhelmed by floodwater, not defeated in battle; this has caused no real harm to the great affairs of the state. Now that relations between Sun and Liu have broken down, Yunchang’s success is certain to displease Sun Quan. Your Majesty may send an envoy to Eastern Wu to explain the advantages and dangers, and have Sun Quan secretly raise troops to strike Yunchang from behind. Promise that when the affair is settled, territory south of the river will be ceded to enfeoff Sun Quan; then the peril of Fan Castle will resolve itself.” Chief Clerk Jiang Ji said, “Zhongda’s counsel is sound. An envoy should be sent to Eastern Wu at once; there is no need to move the capital and unsettle the people.” Cao Cao accepted their counsel and abandoned the plan to move the capital; then he sighed and told his generals, “Yu Jin has followed me for thirty years. Who would have expected him, when danger came, to prove inferior to Pang De! While I send an envoy with a letter to Eastern Wu, I must also find a great general capable of withstanding Yunchang’s onslaught.” Before he had finished, a general below the steps stepped forward and answered, “I am willing to go.” Cao Cao looked and saw that it was Xu Huang. Cao Cao was delighted. He assigned fifty thousand elite troops, appointed Xu Huang commander with Lü Jian as his deputy, and ordered them to march on the appointed day and encamp at Yanglingpo; they were to wait for a response from the southeast before advancing.

p.src: Now Sun Quan received Cao Cao’s letter and, after reading it, gladly agreed. He wrote a reply and sent the envoy back ahead of him, then assembled his civil and military officers for counsel. Zhang Zhao said, “I recently heard that Yunchang captured Yu Jin and beheaded Pang De, and that his might has shaken the realm, so much so that Cao Cao wished to move the capital to avoid his onslaught. Now Fan Castle is in desperate peril and Cao Cao has sent an envoy seeking aid, but once the matter is settled, I fear he may go back on his word.” Before Sun Quan could speak, word suddenly came that Lü Meng had arrived from Lukou in a small boat and wished to report urgent business in person. Sun Quan summoned him and asked what it was. Lü Meng said, “Yunchang has now led his army away to besiege Fan Castle. We can take advantage of his absence and seize Jingzhou by surprise.” Sun Quan asked, “What if I were to take Xuzhou in the north?” Lü Meng replied, “Cao Cao is now far away in Hebei and has no leisure to look east. Xuzhou has few defenders and could certainly be taken if we went; yet its terrain favors land warfare, not naval warfare, and even if we took it, it would be difficult to defend. Better to take Jingzhou first, gain complete control of the Yangtze, and then devise a greater plan.” Sun Quan said, “My true intention was to take Jingzhou; I spoke as I did only to test you. Quickly devise a plan for me. I shall raise my army and follow soon afterward.” Lü Meng took leave of Sun Quan and returned to Lukou. Scouts were already reporting, “All along the river, at intervals of twenty or thirty li, beacon towers stand upon every height.” Hearing also that Jingzhou’s forces were disciplined and fully prepared, Lü Meng exclaimed in alarm, “If so, it cannot be taken quickly. In the heat of the moment, I urged the Marquis of Wu to seize Jingzhou. What am I to do now?” Unable to devise a plan despite much thought, he feigned illness and withdrew from public view, sending a man to report back to Sun Quan. When Sun Quan heard that Lü Meng was ill, he was deeply displeased. Lu Xun stepped forward and said, “Lü Ziming’s illness is a pretense, not a true sickness.” Sun Quan said, “Since Boyan knows it to be a pretense, you may go and visit him.”

p.src: Lu Xun accepted the command and reached the camp at Lukou that night. When he went to see Lü Meng, he found that there was indeed no sign of illness in his face. Lu Xun said, “By order of the Marquis of Wu, I have respectfully come to inquire after Ziming’s illness.” Lü Meng said, “It is only a slight indisposition. Why trouble yourself to inquire after me?” Lu Xun said, “The Marquis of Wu has entrusted you with a grave responsibility. Why do you let the opportunity pass without acting and merely brood in frustration?” Lü Meng fixed his eyes on Lu Xun and remained silent for a long while. Lu Xun continued, “I have a modest prescription that may cure the general’s ailment, though I do not know whether it can be used.” Lü Meng dismissed his attendants and asked, “Boyan, if you have a good remedy, pray instruct me at once.” Lu Xun smiled and said, “Ziming’s ailment arises from nothing more than the strict order of Jingzhou’s troops and the beacon towers prepared along the river. I have a plan that will leave the guards along the river unable to light their beacons; then the troops of Jingzhou will have no choice but to surrender. What say you?” Lü Meng exclaimed in astonished gratitude, “Boyan, your words show that you see into my very heart. I beg to hear your excellent plan.” Lu Xun said, “Yunchang relies upon his heroic prowess and considers himself invincible; the only man he fears is you, General. Take this opportunity to feign illness and resign your post, yielding the command at Lukou to another. Have that man address Lord Guan with humble words and lavish praise, thereby feeding his pride. He will surely withdraw all the troops from Jingzhou and send them toward Fancheng. Once Jingzhou is left undefended, a single force using an unexpected stratagem can seize it by surprise, and Jingzhou will be in the palm of our hand.” Lü Meng was overjoyed. “A truly excellent plan!” he cried.

p.src: Thereupon Lü Meng took to his bed on the pretense of illness and submitted a memorial resigning his post. Lu Xun returned to Sun Quan and related the entire plan. Sun Quan then summoned Lü Meng back to Jianye to recuperate. When Lü Meng arrived, he entered Sun Quan’s presence. Sun Quan asked, “As for the command at Lukou, in former days Zhou Gongjin recommended Lu Zijing to succeed him; later Zijing recommended you as his own successor. Now you too must recommend a man of both outstanding talent and high reputation to replace you. That would be best.” Lü Meng replied, “If we employ a man of great reputation, Yunchang will certainly be on his guard. Lu Xun is a man of profound designs, yet his name is not widely known, so Yunchang will feel no fear of him. If he is appointed to take my place, the enterprise will surely prosper.” Sun Quan was delighted and that very day appointed Lu Xun General of the Household Who Assists and Right Area Commander, charging him with guarding Lukou in Lü Meng’s stead. Lu Xun declined, saying, “I am young and unlearned; I fear I am unequal to so great a charge.” Sun Quan said, “Ziming has vouched for you; he cannot be mistaken. You must not refuse.” Lu Xun then bowed and accepted the seals of office, and traveled through the night to Lukou. After completing the transfer of the cavalry, infantry, and naval forces, he immediately composed a letter, prepared famous horses, rare brocades, wine, and other gifts, and dispatched an envoy to carry them to Fancheng and present himself to Lord Guan.

p.src: At the time, Lord Guan was recuperating from his arrow wound and keeping his troops inactive. Suddenly a report came: “Lü Meng, the commander guarding Lukou in Jiangdong, is gravely ill. Sun Quan has recalled him for treatment and recently appointed Lu Xun as general to guard Lukou in his place. Lu Xun has now sent a man bearing a letter and gifts, who has come especially to pay his respects.” Lord Guan summoned the envoy and, pointing at him, said, “Zhongmou is shallow in judgment, to appoint this stripling as a general!” The envoy prostrated himself and said, “General Lu has presented this letter and prepared these gifts, first to offer congratulations to Your Lordship, and second to seek amity between our two houses. We humbly beg you to accept them with favor.” Lord Guan opened the letter and read it; its language was exceedingly humble and respectful. When Lord Guan had finished reading, he threw back his head and laughed. He ordered his attendants to accept the gifts and dismissed the envoy to return. The envoy returned to Lu Xun and reported, “Lord Guan was delighted and no longer shows any concern about Jiangdong.”

p.src: Lu Xun was overjoyed. He secretly sent men to investigate and learned that Lord Guan had indeed withdrawn more than half the troops from Jingzhou and ordered them to Fancheng, intending to advance as soon as his arrow wound was healed. Having learned all the particulars, Lu Xun immediately sent a man to report them to Sun Quan with all speed through the night. Sun Quan summoned Lü Meng and consulted him, saying, “Now that Yunchang has indeed withdrawn the troops of Jingzhou to attack Fancheng, we can devise a plan to seize Jingzhou by surprise. What if you and my younger kinsman Sun Jiao lead the main army there together?” Sun Jiao, whose courtesy name was Shuming, was the second son of Sun Quan’s uncle Sun Jing. Lü Meng replied, “My lord, if you deem me fit for use, then employ me alone; if you deem Shuming fit, then employ Shuming alone. Have you not heard how Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu once served as Left and Right Area Commanders? Although decisions rested with Yu, Pu considered himself a veteran minister placed beneath Yu, and the two were far from harmonious. Only after Pu witnessed Yu’s abilities did he come to respect and submit to him. My abilities fall short of Yu’s, while Shuming’s kinship with you is closer than Pu’s standing was. I fear we may not be able to work together successfully.”

p.src: Sun Quan understood at once and appointed Lü Meng Commander-in-Chief, granting him supreme authority over all the forces of Jiangdong. He ordered Sun Jiao to remain in the rear and provide support with provisions. All wore white garments and worked the oars on deck, while picked soldiers lay hidden inside the || boats. Next he ordered the seven great generals Han Dang, Jiang Qin, Zhu Ran, Pan Zhang, Zhou Tai, Xu Sheng, and Ding Feng to advance one after another. All the remaining forces stayed with the Marquis of Wu to serve as reserves and reinforcements. On one hand, an envoy was sent with a letter to Cao Cao, urging him to advance and strike Yunchang from the rear. On the other, Lu Xun was notified in advance; then the men in white set out in their swift boats toward the Xunyang reaches of the river. They pressed onward day and night until they reached the northern bank. When the guards at a riverside beacon tower challenged them, the men of Wu replied, “We are all traveling merchants. The wind has held us back on the river, so we have come here to take shelter.” They then presented goods to the soldiers guarding the tower. The soldiers believed them and allowed them to moor by the river.

p.src: At about the second watch, all the picked troops inside the || emerged and bound the officers and soldiers atop the beacon tower. At a single secret signal, the troops aboard the more than eighty boats rose together and seized the garrisons at every strategically important beacon post, taking them all aboard without allowing a single man to escape. They then drove swiftly onward and made straight for Jingzhou without anyone becoming aware of them. As they neared Jingzhou, Lü Meng soothed the government troops captured at the riverside posts with kind words and richly rewarded each of them. He ordered them to trick the guards into opening the city gates and then light a fire as the signal. The soldiers accepted the order, and Lü Meng had them lead the way. By midnight they had reached the foot of the walls and called for the gate to be opened. The gatekeepers recognized them as soldiers of Jingzhou and opened the gates. With a single shout, the soldiers rushed forward and lit the signal fire inside the gate. The troops of Wu poured in together and seized Jingzhou by surprise. Lü Meng immediately issued an order throughout the army: “Anyone who wantonly kills a single person or takes a single article from the people shall assuredly be punished under military law.” The existing officials were all retained in their former posts. Lord Guan’s family was lodged separately in another residence, and no idlers were permitted to disturb them. Meanwhile, a man was sent to report the victory to Sun Quan.

p.src: One day, during heavy rain, Lü Meng mounted his horse and led several riders on an inspection of the four gates. Suddenly he saw a man take a bamboo-leaf rain hat from a commoner to cover his armor. Lü Meng shouted for his attendants to seize the man and questioned him; he proved to be a fellow native of Lü Meng’s home district. Lü Meng said, “Though you are my fellow countryman, my order has already been issued. You have knowingly violated it and must be dealt with under military law.” The man pleaded through his tears, “I feared the rain would soak the government-issued armor, so I took the hat to cover it, not for my private use. I beg you, General, to remember the ties of our common homeland.” Lü Meng said, “I know full well that you meant to cover government armor, but you still ought not to have taken anything belonging to the people.” He sternly ordered his attendants to drag the man away and behead him. After the severed head had been displayed as a warning, Lü Meng had the man’s remains gathered and buried them with tears. From that time onward, the entire army was awed into strict discipline.

p.src: Before many days had passed, Sun Quan arrived at the head of his men. Lü Meng went outside the city to welcome him and escorted him into the government offices. After Sun Quan had commended and rewarded him, he retained Pan Jun as Administrative Officer and placed the affairs of Jingzhou in his charge; he released Yu Jin from confinement and sent him back to Cao Cao, reassured the people, rewarded the troops, and gave a celebratory banquet. Sun Quan said to Lü Meng, “We have now taken Jingzhou, but Fu Shiren holds Gong'an and Mi Fang holds Nanjun. How are we to recover these two places?” Before he had finished, a man suddenly stepped forward and said, “There is no need to draw a bow or loose an arrow. With this three-inch tongue of mine, I shall persuade Fu Shiren of Gong'an to come and surrender. Will that suffice?” All looked and saw that it was Yu Fan. Sun Quan said, “Zhongxiang, what good plan have you for inducing Fu Shiren to surrender?” Yu Fan replied, “I have been on close terms with Shiren since childhood. If I now explain to him where his advantage and peril lie, he is certain to submit.” Sun Quan was delighted and accordingly gave Yu Fan five hundred soldiers, with whom he hastened straight to Gong'an.

p.src: Now Fu Shiren, hearing that Jingzhou had fallen, hastily ordered the city gates closed and prepared a stout defense. When Yu Fan arrived and found the gates tightly shut, he wrote a letter, tied it to an arrow, and shot it into the city. A soldier picked it up and presented it to Fu Shiren. Shiren opened and read the letter; it urged him to surrender. When he had finished reading, he recalled the resentment Lord Guan had shown toward him upon departing and thought it better to surrender without delay; he immediately ordered the gates thrown wide and invited Yu Fan into the city. After the two had exchanged courtesies, each spoke of their old friendship. Yu Fan told him of the Marquis of Wu's magnanimity and generosity, and of the honor and humility with which he treated worthy men. Shiren was overjoyed and at once accompanied Yu Fan to Jingzhou, bringing his seal and insignia with him to surrender. Sun Quan was greatly pleased and ordered him to return to the defense of Gong'an. Lü Meng privately said to Sun Quan, “Yunchang has not yet been captured. If Shiren is left at Gong'an, trouble is certain to arise in time. It would be better to send him to Nanjun to persuade Mi Fang to surrender.” Sun Quan therefore summoned Fu Shiren and said, “Mi Fang is a close friend of yours. Go and persuade him to surrender, and I shall reward you handsomely.” Fu Shiren readily accepted the command and, leading a little over ten horsemen, went straight to Nanjun to induce Mi Fang to submit.
